finding.claim: The /settings/email state-changing endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid=None. The account email change is not protected by authentication. If set_email treats a None uid as a real or default record, the change could affect it. Even otherwise, the endpoint should reject anonymous callers. The sibling /settings/password route correctly uses login_required.
finding.source: Unauthenticated POST request to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, a protected account-modification operation

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None for anonymous users, and does not abort
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with uid None

finding.guards_checked: login_required is not applied; login_optional never aborts. No other auth check in the handler. No CSRF protection is visible in this file (POST with session cookie). The set_email body is a stub, so exact impact depends on the real implementation. The neighbouring /settings/password route uses login_required.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid and never aborts; no auth check in change_email)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password's login_required at routes.py:11-12; set_email is a stub (routes.py:48), so the real impact is unknown, but the missing auth on a state-changing endpoint is real.
